en: The vessels are human vessels—
Nārada, the divine seer.
Vasudeva— the father of Kṛṣṇa—
and Nandagopa, the superintendent of Gokula and friend of Vasudeva.
Ugrasena was the father of Kaṃsa;
Dāmodara Śrīkṛṣṇa was the son of Vasudeva;
and Saṃkarṣaṇa was the son of Vasudeva.
Garuḍa is the vehicle of Viṣṇu;
the weapons of Viṣṇu are the conch, the sword Nandaka, the discus, and the Śārṅga bow;
Kaṃsa was the king of Mathurā.
Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika were Kaṃsa’s wrestlers; Bhaṭa was Kaṃsa’s soldier; Kañcukī was Kaṃsa’s chamberlain.
Śāpa was the superintendent of all guards;
his son was Kuṇḍodara, who was the servant of Kātyāyanī.
Śūla,
Nīla,
and Manojava.
Vṛddhagopālaka, Dāmaka,
and Ariṣṭarṣabha are specific types of Asuras.
Kāliya was a great serpent dwelling in the Yamunā;
Strīpātraṇi refers to Devakī, the mother of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The female door-keeper—the nurse of Devakī;
the foster-mother of Māyājālikā;
and all the young Caṇḍāla women.
Kātyāyanī—the goddess of all; Ghoṣasundarīs—the deities of the kingdom; Rājaśrī—the goddess of sovereignty.
Madhukarikā, the female doorkeeper— the female doorkeeper Yaśodharā of Kaṃsa—
[end of] the first act.
(At the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* enters.
*Sūtradhāra*:

In the former Kṛta age, he was named Nārāyaṇa, with a body white as a conch or milk; in the Tretā age, he is Viṣṇu, possessing a golden luster, who established the three worlds upon his three strides.

May that Dāmodara protect you—He who, at the time of Rāvaṇa’s slaughter, resembled the dark-green hue of durvā grass, and who in the Dvāpara age was ever like the color of collyrium, [and who in the Kali age is likewise present]. || 1 ||
Thus I inform the noble sirs. Ah! While I am occupied in making this request, what is this sound that is heard? Pray, let me look!
(Behind the scenes) I am Gaganasañcārī!
The Stage Manager: Very well, I understand.
This rain of flowers falls, and the musical instruments of the gods resound.
This Nārada has arrived swiftly to see Hari, who was born in the Vṛṣṇi clan.
(Exit. [End of the introductory scene. Then enters Nārada.
Nārada said:
"I am Nārada, who wanders through the sky and am renowned throughout the three worlds; having come here from the world of Brahmā, I am one who delights in quarreling."
O friend!
Now that the conflicts between the gods and asuras have ceased and all is eternally peaceful, I find no delight in the intermediate space.
For during my intervals of Vedic study, I strike both the lute strings and my own enmities. || 4 ||
Moreover,
I have supreme devotion to the words spoken by my grandfather, and all the penance groves are highly esteemed by me.
I speak the truth: held in the tips of my fingers, the lute and enmities—terrible and harsh quarrels—are dear to me.

Therefore, I have come here to behold the Blessed One, the beginning of the worlds, without end or decay, who was born in the Vṛṣṇi clan for the welfare of the world and for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa—Nārāyaṇa himself. Ah! Here is the lady Devakī, having taken up with Vasudeva the Lord of the Three Worlds who has assumed childhood through his illusory power (māyā), slowly departing from her own home.
She is the teacher of the gods and the granter of fearlessness to the worlds.

Afflicted by grief, the moon-faced woman, having become tranquil at night, bore with her two arms the one whose hand holds a discus— the slayer of the Daityas— like Mount Mandara, the best of mountains.
This, this is the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, of infinite prowess, with eyes as long as lotuses, the protector of the lords of the gods, the slayer of the strength of the asuras.
The banner of the three worlds, the creator of the universe, the sustainer of people, the primordial Puruṣa. || 7 ||

Alas! This which has arisen is the very root of strife. Therefore, I too shall circumambulate the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa and proceed directly to the world of Brahmā. Homage to the Blessed One, the cause of the three worlds;
to Nārāyaṇa, the supreme refuge of the world of men, the protector of the worlds, whose eyes are as pure as lotuses.
Salutations to Rāma, the hero who brought down Rāvaṇa and Virocana, the abode of valor, the most excellent one. || 8 ||
(Exit. (Then enters Devakī with a child in her hand.
Devakī:

Alas! Though I witness these great omens arising at the very moment of my son's birth, which portend his great majesty, and though I reflect upon the destruction of Kaṃsa, I, unfortunate as I am, do not fully believe it. Where indeed has my noble husband gone? (Walking about and looking ahead) Oh, here is my noble husband coming this very way, his eyes wide with joy and wonder.

He is coming! (Alas! Though I am witnessing with my own eyes the great omens that arose at the time of my son's birth, which would have indicated his great majesty, I do not fully believe it, unfortunate as I am, as I reflect upon the cruelty of that wretched Kaṃsa. Where has my noble husband gone? Oh, here comes my noble husband from this very direction, his eyes wide with joy and wonder!
(Then Vasudeva enters.)
Vasudeva—(Reflectively) Oh! What indeed is this?
Lightning flashes in the sky, the earth trembles with the roars of fresh clouds driven by fierce winds.
But here in this world, it is certain that Viṣṇu, the slayer of the hosts of asuras, has now descended for the sake of protecting all creatures. || 9 ||
(Looking) Here is Devakī;
disregarding all fatigue, she goes forth for the sake of the destruction of her six sons, protecting the seventh.
Driven by greed for many virtues, she carries the death of Kaṃsa—who was designated as "son" at the time of his birth due to omens.
Devakī—
(Approaching) Victory to my noble son!
Vasudeva—
Devakī: It is indeed midnight. Everyone in Mathurā is fast asleep. Therefore, before anyone sees us, let me take the child and depart.
Devakī:
Where will my noble husband take him?
Vasudeva:

O Devakī, you speak the truth; I too do not know. However, the evil-minded Kaṃsa commands the entire earth under his single umbrella. Therefore, where indeed shall this long-lived child be taken? Or rather, I shall take the boy and depart for wherever destiny shall ordain.
Devakī:
Noble husband, I wish first to see him well.
Vasudeva: [Listens.]
O you who are so affectionate toward your son!
Why look at this moon within the orb of Rāhu’s mouth?
Even though it has been well-beheld by you, Kaṃsa shall become its death.
Devakī:
It shall not happen under any circumstances.
Vasudeva:—
"Whatever you have said, let that be said by all the gods. Bring him!
Devakī:
"Let my noble husband take him. (May my noble husband take him.)
Vasudeva—(Taking him up): Oh, the weight of this child! Well done;
this lotus-eyed boy possesses the essential strength of the Vindhya and Mandara mountains.
By her the glorious one was held in the womb; oh, what fortitude indeed belongs to women! 12.
Devakī! Enter the inner apartments.
Devakī: Here I go, unfortunate as I am. (She exits. (Here I go, unfortunate as I am.)
Vasudeva: This is Devakī;
she goes there as if divided in two—here with her heart, and there with her limbs.
Just as the crescent moon appears divided into two, both in the sky and in the water. || 13 ||

Ah, Devakī has entered! Now I too shall take refuge at the city gate. Here I am, O sirs; having seized the child, my anger born from the destruction of my first son tempered by the fear of the king, I hasten here along the path, carrying him with both arms like Mount Mandara.

(Walking about) Here is the city gate. I shall enter. (Entering) Ah! Everyone in Mathurā is fast asleep. I shall depart. (Walking about) I have left Mathurā. Oh, how powerful this darkness is! For now:
The darkness seems to smear my limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium.
Like service rendered to a wicked person, my vision has come to fruitionlessness. || 15 ||
Oh, the power of darkness!
The quarters of the sky appear as if devoid of light, and the trees seem as if solidified;
a transformation of form has been wrought upon the well-settled world. (16)

I am not able to go. Oh, the light of a lamp! Could it be that the wicked Kaṃsa, having learned of my departure, has come surrounded by lamps to seize me? Very well, I shall quell his pride. When the world was shrouded in darkness and I could not see my path,
the prince created a light for the purpose of my departure.

This is the path; I shall now depart. Ah! Here stands the divine Yamunā, filled with dark waters. Alas, my labor has been in vain! What shall I do now? Very well, I have found a way. This river is teeming with crocodiles and serpents, garlanded with great waves, and difficult to cross even in thought.
If fate stands by me, I shall swiftly carry out this success, though distressed by the failure of my purpose, using only my arms as a raft.

(Having done so, with astonishment) Ah! The water is split in two; it stands here and flows there. The blessed lady has granted me a path. I shall now withdraw. (Descending) I have emerged from the Yamunā. Oh! A sound like a "huṃ" is heard. Clearly, this unfortunate one is near the cowherd station. Ah! And here, near the station, my friend Nandagopa resides. He indeed—

"I was bound and whipped at Kaṃsa’s command; now, if I enter, the cowherds will suspect that Vasudeva has entered during the night. Therefore, I shall wait for the break of dawn here beneath this banyan tree. O deities of the banyan tree! If this boy has indeed been born in the Vṛṣṇi clan for the welfare of the world and for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa, let someone from the settlement come here. No, no—let my friend Nanda the cowherd come."
(Then enters Nandagopa, carrying the girl.
Nandagopa:
(With grief) Child! Child! Why now, having left the house unguarded, do you go away, abandoning us? For at this moment, the onset of the buffalo-demon is indeed powerful.
The night, like a blind well, remains with its light destroyed by the foul weather; it is a time of closed eyes,
like a cowherd woman who has fallen asleep in the rain, her blue garment drenched.
Today, at the third watch of the night, this daughter was born to our housewife Yaśodā. As soon as she was born, this poor child fell unconscious.

Tomorrow, there will be a festival in our cowherd settlement called Indrayajña. Therefore, lest this sorrow be experienced by the cowherds, I alone, with my feet bound by heavy chains, shall take this girl.
I have departed. Even the virtuous Yaśodā does not know that her child or daughter has been born; she has fallen into a swoon. Daughter! Daughter! (Daughter! Daughter!
Why now do you depart without sporting with the household fortune and without leaving it behind? For now the darkness is powerful, like the onset of a hundred buffaloes;
the night has arrived, its form obscured, with its moonlight destroyed by foul weather.
She was like a cowherd girl who had fallen asleep while her blue garment was still wrapped around her.

"For today at midnight, this daughter was born to our family by my wife Yaśodā; yet as soon as she was born, this poor girl has passed away. Tomorrow, there will be a festival called the Indra-sacrifice, which is customary for our village. Therefore, lest this sorrow be experienced by the cowherd folk, I have taken this girl and departed alone, with my feet heavy with fetters. My poor Yaśodā, too, does not even know whether a boy or a girl was born; she has fallen into a swoon. Daughter! Daughter!"
Vāsudeva:
Who indeed is this lamenting at night? This poor soul is surely a fellow-student of mine.
Nandagopa: [He is.]
"Why now, after not having enjoyed the fortune of our home, do you depart from here without even leaving us?
Vasudeva:
"I recognize you by your voice; you must be my friend Nandagopa. I shall call out to him. Friend Nandagopa! This way, please!"

Nandagopa—(With fear) Alas! Who is it now that addresses me with a voice as familiar as one heard before, crying "Nandagopa! Nandagopa!"? Is it a demon, or perhaps a Piśāca? In such a terrifying hour, Madalika’s daughter is in my hands; what indeed shall I do? (Alas! Who is it now that addresses me with a voice as familiar as one heard before, crying "Nandagopa! Nandagopa!")
He calls out: "Is this a *rākṣasa*, or perhaps a *piśāca*? In such a terrifying night, this dead girl is in my hands; what indeed shall I do?
Vasudeva:
"Friend Nandagopa! Enough of this suspicion. Come this way."

Nandagopa—(Listening intently) Ah! By the sound of his voice, I recognize the noble Vāsudeva. I shall approach him. Or rather, what business have I with him? By this servant of Kaṃsa, having repeated the King’s words, I was seized, beaten, and bound with fetters. Therefore, I will not go. Or rather, shame on my own nature! I have been made a vessel for his virtues; I suffer in his suffering and rejoice in his joy.
Very well; nevertheless, I shall remember the execution of the single-bonding by the King’s command. I will approach. Here is the child. What shall I do? Very well, I shall do this much first.

(Approaching and looking about, with astonishment) Dawn has broken! There stands the noble Vasudeva holding the child. (Approaching) Victory to the noble one! Victory! (Ah! By the sound of his voice, it is the noble Vasudeva.)

I know; yet I shall approach him. Or rather, what business have I there? Having heard the words of King Kaṃsa, I offended him and was beaten with whips and bound with fetters. Therefore, I will not go. Or rather, shame on my cruelty! Though he has performed a thousand favors for me, and grieves in my grief and rejoices in my joy, even so do I remember the single bond imposed by the king’s command.
"I shall go up to him. This is the cave. What shall I do? Very well, I will act in this way. The night has turned to dawn. Here stands my lord Vasudeva, holding the child. Victory to my lord!
Victory!
Vasudeva:
Friend Nandagopa! Is all well with the blessed cows?
Nandagopa:
Yes, my lord! All is well.
Nandagopa:
Yes, my lord! All is well. (Ām bhartaḥ! Kuśalam.
Vasudeva:
Now, is all well with your household?
Nandagopa:
As for the household—yes, master! All is well. (As for the household—yes, sir! All is well.)
Vasudeva:
Friend! Why is this being concealed now?
Nandagopa: [He speaks.]
"Master! There is nothing.
Vasudeva:
"By my very life, you would be under a curse if you do not speak the truth."

Nandagopa: What can be done? Listen, sir. This morning at the third watch, this child was born to our housewife—not indeed, not indeed, to your slave girl Yaśodā. As soon as she was born, this little girl became one whose life-breath had departed. Tomorrow, there will be a festival called Indrayajña celebrated in our cowherd settlement. Therefore, I [have done this] so that the cowherds do not have to experience this sorrow.

With my feet fettered by heavy shackles, I have emerged after breaking open this basket. The poor Yaśodā did not even know whether it was a boy or a girl; she fell into a swoon. (What recourse is there? Let my master listen. At midnight today, this daughter—no, no, rather your servant Yaśodā—gave birth, and this wretched girl, as soon as she was born, has passed away.

"Tomorrow there will be for our village a festival called the Indra-sacrifice, which is appropriate for us. Therefore, lest this sorrow experienced by the cowherd folk be felt by me alone, I have taken this girl and departed with my feet heavy with fetters. Even the poor Yaśodā does not know whether a boy or a girl has been born; she has fallen into a state of confusion.
Vasudeva—
Alas, sir! It is not possible to deceive Fate, who is the very foundation of the world. Friend! Let this body, which has become like wood, be abandoned.
Nandagopa:
I cannot, my lord! I cannot! (na śaknomi bhartaḥ! na śaknomi!)
Vasudeva: Such is the way of the world; let it be abandoned.
Nandagopa: [He speaks.]
"As my lord commands! O girl! O girl! (Thus she weeps.
Vasudeva:
"Friend! Enough, enough with weeping! Arise, arise!"
Nandagopa—(Having done so, he approaches) Victory to my lord! What is to be done by this servant?
Vasudeva—
Friend! Do you not also know that my six sons were brought to their death by the wicked Kaṃsa?
Nandagopa:
I know it, sir! I know it! (jānāmi bhartaḥ! jānāmi.)
Vasudeva:
Therefore, this long-lived one is the seventh. I have no further fortune among my sons; let him be taken so that he may live by your good fortune.
Nandagopa: [Accepts.]

I am afraid, my lord! I am afraid! If King Kaṃsa hears that Vasudeva’s son has been deposited as a trust in the hands of the cowherd Nanda—well, what need is there for more words? My head is already lost!
Vasudeva:
(To himself) Alas, the task is ruined! These cruel men are indeed mindful of what has been said to them. Therefore, I shall speak thus. (Aloud) Friend Nandagopa!
If I have ever done anything for you in the past, the time has now arrived for you to repay that favor.
Nandagopa:
What, what is the recompense?
Whether it be Kaṃsa, or even Kaṃsa’s father Ugrasena—let my lord bring the boy here.
Vasudeva:
Friend, take it!
Nandagopa: [takes it]...

"Master! I am defiled; I have taken hold of a dead girl. Let the Master wait a moment while I go to the waters of the Yamunā and perform purification. Vasudeva: (Bhartṛḥ! aśaucito 'smi, mṛtā dārikā gṛhītā | muhūrtakaṃ pratipālayatu bhartā yāvad yamunājalaṃ gatvā śaucaṃ karomi ||) Vasudeva:
Friend! By nature, you are indeed pure from living in the cowherd settlement.
Nandagopa:
Therefore, I shall perform for you that purification with dust which is appropriate for our settlement.
Vasudeva:
What is the harm in this? Let the purification be performed.
Nandagopa: [He does so.]

"As the master commands. (Doing so, with astonishment) "A marvel, a marvel, O Master! A marvel! While he was searching for dust, a stream of water as wide as a yoke rose up, piercing the earth! Vasudeva:
"It is indeed the power of a child. Perform the purification rites.
Nandagopa: "Master! So be it. (Having done so, he approaches: "Master! Here I am."
Vasudeva:
Let it be taken.
Nandagopa: [Let it be taken.]
"O Lord! My arms are exceedingly weak; they are not capable of holding this child who is like Mount Mandara.
Vasudeva:
"Friend! You are indeed possessed of great strength and prowess."
Nandagopa:

Let my lord hear my strength and prowess! When a bull was tearing [the ground], I took hold of its horn and released it; I pushed aside carts laden with merchandise that were stuck in the mud. Such as I am now, I am not capable of seizing this boy.
I swear it! At present, I am not capable of seizing such a child.
(Then enter the five weapons and Garuḍa.
Garuḍa:—
I am Suparṇa Garuḍa, possessed of great speed; I am the chariot and the banner of this wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
For in former times, during the conflicts between the gods and the asuras—
O, by the power of Viṣṇu, I carry Viṣṇu.
Cakra said:
"I am Cakra, adorning the tip of Kṛṣṇa’s hand, possessing fierce splendor like the midday sun."
During the three strides and during the churning for the nectar of immortality, the hosts of Dānavas and Daityas were slain by me.
Śārṅgī: O Śārṅga, I am a woman whose well-rounded waist is clasped by the hand of Viṣṇu; yet, through my physical form, I possess the pride of the strength and virility of a man.
For whose sake, at the front of battles, I have shattered the hosts of enemies, their elephants, chariots, horses, and men having been utterly routed.
Kaumodakī:
The mace named Kaumodakī belongs to Hari;
having crushed all enemies by my command, [it remains].
I sported in the rivers of blood of the Dānavas slain by me in battle.
Śaṅkha said:
"I am indeed Śaṅkha, personally upraised from the Ocean of Milk by Viṣṇu himself;
by my sound, those enemies of the gods shall perish in battle. (24)
Nandaka: I am Nandaka; there is no one who turns his back on me in battles.
I go forth by the power of the mighty Viṣṇu, whose name is ever remembered.
Cakra said:
"We are the discus, the bow Śārṅga, the mace, the conch, and the sword Nandaka—slayers of the Daityas—who have arrived as the attendants of Vāsudeva for the sake of his mission. (27)

Therefore, please come. We too shall descend to the world of men and, disguised in the dress of cowherds, enter the settlement (*ghoṣa*) itself in order to follow the childhood exploits of the Blessed Viṣṇu who has descended there.
All:
So be it. (They approach Viṣṇu.)
Vasudeva:
Friend! Let him pay homage while he is still a child.
Nandagopa: [He does so.]
"O Lord! So be it! O Prince! Salutations to you, salutations to you! Indeed, enough! Save yourself by your own self. What power or prowess do we cowherds have to seize you? Cakra:—
Homage to the Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa! O Blessed One, Mahāviṣṇu!
Many deeds, both to be done and not to be done, by the gods and the asuras will come to pass in the world through you.
Therefore, O banner of the Yadu dynasty, show favor to these people who have become so wretched! (28)
Vasudeva:
Let it be taken.
Nandagopa: [Let it be taken.]
"As my lord commands. (He takes it. (Yad bhartājñāpayati |) Vasudeva: Friend! Dawn has broken. May you return.
Nandagopa:— How wonderful, how wonderful, O Lord! How wonderful! These two have fallen into their bonds!
Vasudeva:—
"All this is the power of the Prince. May you turn back.
Nandagopa:
"As the Lord commands."
Vasudeva:
Or rather, come here for a moment.
Nandagopa: [approaches]
"Master! Here I am. Vāsudeva:
"I know you to be naturally affectionate toward me at all times."
Even at this time, a deep-rooted affection for him is observed;
it is for the sake of preserving the Yādavas that only a small remnant of what was once largely consumed remains like a sown seed.

"What will you do for the prince? Nandagopa replied: "Listen, sir! He goes to one house and drinks milk; he goes to another house and eats curd; he goes to yet another house and swallows fresh butter; he goes to another house..."

He drinks milk; having gone to one house, he eats curd; having gone to another house, he swallows butter; having gone to yet another house, he eats rice-pudding; having gone to another house, he looks at a jar of buttermilk. What more need be said? He becomes the master of our entire cowherd settlement. (Let my lord listen: having gone to one house, he drinks milk;

having gone to another house, he will eat curd; having gone to another house, he swallows butter; having gone to another house, he eats rice-pudding; having gone to another house, he looks at a jar of buttermilk. What more need be said? He becomes the master of our cowherd settlement.)
Vasudeva:
So be it. May you return. Nandagopa: [He departs.]
"As Your Honor commands. (Exit. (Yad bhartājñāpayati |) Vasudeva:

Surely Nanda the cowherd has already departed; therefore, I too shall go to Mathurā itself. (Walking about) A sound like weeping is heard. Could it be that Nanda the cowherd has actually returned out of fear of Kaṃsa?

(Walking about) Ah! This girl has regained her life-breaths. Now, taking her and placing her in Devakī’s hands, I shall deceive the evil-minded Kaṃsa. (Taking her) Oh, the weight of this child! Even this is something quite different from the prince; it is a great being. Now, I shall pass by. Ah! Here is the blessed Yamunā standing just as before. Now, I shall withdraw. I have emerged from the Yamunā.

This is the city gate. All the people in Mathurā are likewise fast asleep; I shall enter. (Entering) This is indeed the house of the wicked Kaṃsa, which appears as if it were presided over by old age. But this, our own house, appears as if it were ascended by Fortune. "You shall know in due time. The King: [listens].

"Let play be made!

"What has been born? The Chamberlain: "A girl has been born."

Carrying this body emaciated by grief,

"As the Blessed Lady commands. (Kātyāyanī exits with her retinue.

"May there be peace, may there be peace for us and for our cattle-wealth!

Moreover, this is another marvel. Ten days after his birth, a demoness named Pūtanā, whose breasts were filled with poison, assumed the form of Nanda’s wife and arrived. Recognizing him, the virtuous woman [Nanda’s wife] threw her down; the demoness, being crushed by the weight of her own skin, perished right there. Thereafter, the cowherd Nanda was filled with joy.

Indeed, having assumed the disguise of a Śabara, he arrived as a Dānava; knowing him to be such, he was ground to dust with a single kick of his foot, and even that Dānava died right there. Then, disguised as Māṣapaṭu and Nandagopaṭu, he goes to one house and drinks milk, goes to another house and eats curd, goes to one house and swallows butter, and goes to another house...

He ate his meal and went to another’s house, where he looked into a jar of oil. Then, by the young cowherd women who were dancing, it was told to Nanda’s wife. Then Nanda’s wife, having taken a rope and tied it in the middle of it, fastened the other end to a mortar. Then, seeing that mortar being struck, she placed the demon named Yamala-Arjuna [into it]. Then the two became one. Of them—

While Nandagopa was walking along the path, he crushed the roots and branches by trampling them; those demons were likewise destroyed right there. Then the cowherds said, "From this day forward, let the noble son of Dama be known by the name Mahābala-pralakrama. Thereafter, as soon as the cowherd Nanda had finished his meal, the demon named Palamba assumed the guise of Nandagopa.

[He] arrived. Then, perceiving that he was seizing Śaṅkukarṇa by the neck, the Lord Śaṅkukarṇa struck the head of that demon with a blow of his fist. By that blow, that demon, with eyes upturned, died right there; and surrounded by the cowherds, [Śaṅkukarṇa] went to the palm grove to take up the palm-leaf fans. In that palm grove, there was a demon named Dhenuka.

Having assumed the form of a donkey, he arrived. Then, having recognized him, the noble Dāmodara seized his left foot, lifted it up, and struck the palm fruits with it. That demon, too, having revealed himself, was slain right there. Then a demon named Keśin, assuming the form of a camel, arrived. Having recognized him as well, the noble Dāmodara placed his elbow into his mouth. Then, by that [blow], the camel was split in two. He too, having revealed himself as a demon, was slain right there. These and other deeds were performed by the noble Dāmodara. (And this is another marvel.)

When ten nights had passed since the birth of Nanda’s son, a demoness named Pūtanā, whose breasts were filled with poison, came assuming the form of Nanda’s cowherd wife. Then, having taken up the infant, she thrust her breast into his mouth. Realizing who she was, he struck her down while she was asleep; that demoness, having returned to her true form, died right there. Then, when the child was only one month old, a demon named Śakaṭa came, assuming the guise of a cart. Him too—

Having realized this, that Dānava was crushed to pieces by a single kick from the foot and died right then and there. Then, at the end of a month, the son of Nandagopa went to one house and drank milk; having gone to another house, he ate curd;
having gone to one house, he swallowed butter; having gone to another house, he ate milk-rice (*pāyasa*); and having gone to yet another house, he looked into a jar of buttermilk. Then...

The angry cowherd girls said to Nanda’s wife; then the angry Nanda’s wife, taking a rope, tied it around his waist and bound the rest to a mortar. Then, seeing that the mortar had struck against the two *yamalārjuna* trees—the names of two Dānavas who had been cast there—the two trees became joined together. As Nanda’s son passed between them, striking them, they were crushed to powder along with their roots and branches. Those two, having been Dānavas, died right then and there. Then the cowherds said:

"From this day forward, let the one of great strength and prowess be named Bhartṛdāmodara. Then, at the very moment of his running away, a Dānava named Pralamba arrived, having assumed the guise of Nandagopa's son. Seeing him departing while throwing Saṃkarṣaṇa around his neck, the elder brother Saṃkarṣaṇa struck the head of that Dānava with a fist-blow. By that—

With his eyes raised by the blow, that demon also died right then and there. Surrounded by the cowherd folk, [Kṛṣṇa] went to the palm grove to gather palm fruits. There in the palm grove, a demon named Ghenuka, having assumed the form of a donkey, threw down the palm fruits after kicking them up. That demon also died right then and there. Then a demon named Keśin arrived, having assumed the form of a horse; then him also—

Recognizing him, Bhartṛdāmodara seized his left foot, lifted it, and struck down the palm fruits. That Dānava, having been revealed, died right then and there. Then a Dānava named Keśin arrived, assuming the guise of a horse. Recognizing him as well, Bhartṛdāmodara placed his elbow into its mouth; thereupon the horse was split in two by him. That Dānava too, having been revealed, died right then and there.
These and other such deeds were performed by Bhartṛdāmodara.

"As my uncle commands.

bow down every single day with your head bowed low.

dressed in garments of various colors and speaking sweetly,
sport about with their hair-locks adorned with wild blossoms.

some stand there shouting, delighted by their red vesuka-drums and ḍiṇḍima-drums.

others, awakened by the sound in the cowherd settlement and filled with great joy amidst the tumultuous lowing of the cattle, sing with equal delight as they stand within the forest of Vṛndāvana.

Having torn asunder the surface of the earth with his hooves—

Scratching the sky as it were with the rays from the tips of his horns, having assumed the form of a bull and approached for the sake of slaying the enemy,

"Where indeed has Nanda’s cowherd son gone? O Nanda’s cowherd son! Where are you? Dāmodara:

Ariṣṭarṣabha—
(seeing him) Oh,
this boy is indeed full of strength, he who, upon seeing me, so mighty, [acts thus].

"O vile bull! Why do you insult me, thinking I am a child?

Ariṣṭarṣabha:

Dāmodara:—
To lead you to your end—
Ariṣṭarṣabha—
you are capable.

What doubt could there be? Ariṣṭarṣabha: [What doubt could there be?]
"In that case, take up a weapon suited to your own kind.

These two arms of mine, with shoulders as hard as mountain slopes, are my only weapons against those as weak as you;
therefore, being quickly crushed by my staff-like arms—
